title: Which Query Engine? Spark SQL vs SQL Analytics Endpoint vs Warehouse T-SQL vs KQL
purpose: Decide which Fabric query surface a workload should target, branching on read/write need, primary skillset, and data shape.
accessibleSummary: A decision tree with one root question. If the workload must write and needs Spark-native transformation, it routes to Spark SQL in a notebook. If it only needs to query lakehouse Delta tables read-only via T-SQL, it routes to the lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint. If it needs full governed T-SQL with multi-table transactions, it routes to Warehouse T-SQL. If the data is high-volume time-series or log/telemetry data, it routes to KQL against an Eventhouse. A warning node flags the trap of trying to write through the SQL analytics endpoint, which is read-only.
longDescription: This is a decision tree, not a pipeline. Four Fabric query surfaces share overlapping territory — all of them can read Delta data in OneLake — but they differ in read/write capability, primary language, and the workload shape they're built for. The root question asks what the workload actually needs: Spark-native transformation with read/write access routes to Spark SQL, itself one of four interchangeable per-cell languages in a Fabric notebook sharing the same Spark session as PySpark or Scala. Read-only ad hoc querying of already-landed lakehouse Delta tables via T-SQL routes to the auto-provisioned SQL analytics endpoint. A requirement for full governed T-SQL, multi-table ACID transactions, and stored procedures routes to Warehouse. High-volume time-series, log, or telemetry data with sub-second query latency routes to KQL against an Eventhouse. The warning node captures a specific, sourced trap: the SQL analytics endpoint looks like a normal SQL surface but is read-only, so any workload that tries to write through it will fail and needs Warehouse or Spark instead.

nodes.label: What does the query workload need?
nodes.summary: The root question: read/write need, skillset, and data shape decide the engine.
nodes.detail: Before picking a query surface, establish whether the workload needs to write data or only read it, whether the team's skillset is Spark or T-SQL, and whether the data is relational/tabular versus high-volume time-series. These three factors together point to one of four Fabric query engines that otherwise look interchangeable because they can all touch Delta data in OneLake.
nodes.whyItMatters: Picking the wrong surface here means discovering a read/write or governance limitation mid-project rather than at design time — for example choosing the SQL analytics endpoint for a workload that turns out to need writes.

inputs: Whether the workload writes data or only reads it
The team's primary language and skillset (Spark vs T-SQL vs KQL)
Whether the data is relational/tabular or high-volume time-series/telemetry
processing: Determine read-only vs read/write requirement first
Match the team's skillset to a candidate engine
Check whether the data shape (time-series vs relational) overrides the skillset preference
outputs: A routed choice among Spark SQL, the SQL analytics endpoint, Warehouse T-SQL, or KQL
drill.example: A data engineering team building nightly transformations with write-heavy Delta merges routes to Spark SQL; a BI analyst running ad hoc read-only reports against already-landed lakehouse tables routes instead to the SQL analytics endpoint.
controls: Write the read/write requirement down explicitly before comparing engines
failureModes: Choosing an engine by team habit rather than by the workload's actual read/write and data-shape requirements

nodes.label: Spark SQL (notebook cell)
nodes.summary: Spark-native, read/write, shares the notebook's Spark session — pick this for transformation workloads.
nodes.detail: Spark SQL is one of four per-cell languages in a Fabric notebook (alongside PySpark, Scala, and SparkR), switched in with the %%sql magic and executed directly against the notebook's Apache Spark context. It reads and writes Delta tables and is the natural choice when a workload does data engineering-style transformation work, not just ad hoc querying.
nodes.whyItMatters: Because it runs in the same session as PySpark/Scala cells, Spark SQL is the engine to reach for whenever a workload mixes SQL-style aggregation with broader Spark transformation logic in one notebook.

evidence.note: Fabric notebooks support four Apache Spark cell languages — PySpark, Scala, Spark SQL, and SparkR — switched per cell with a language magic command, independent of the notebook's overall primary language.
A %%sql cell executes its query as SparkSQL against the notebook's Apache Spark context, sharing the same running Spark session, cluster, and attached lakehouse as PySpark or Scala cells.

inputs: A transformation workload needing both SQL aggregation and Spark DataFrame/Python logic in one place
processing: Author %%sql cells alongside PySpark cells in the same notebook
Read and write Delta tables directly through the shared Spark session
outputs: Transformed Delta tables written back to the lakehouse, and any read-only reporting queries the same session can also serve
drill.example: A silver-layer notebook uses a %%sql cell to aggregate daily order totals and a PySpark cell immediately after to apply a custom deduplication function to the same DataFrame, both in one session.
controls: Which cell language to use per step — SQL for set-based logic, PySpark/Scala for procedural logic
failureModes: Splitting logically related transformation logic across a %%sql cell and a separate notebook unnecessarily, when both could share one session

nodes.label: Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint
nodes.summary: Read-only T-SQL over lakehouse Delta tables — pick this for ad hoc BI-style querying, never writes.
nodes.detail: Every Fabric lakehouse auto-provisions a companion SQL analytics endpoint that makes any Delta table under Tables/ immediately queryable via T-SQL, with no separate ETL or export step. It shares the same underlying Delta data as the lakehouse's Spark session but is a read-only query surface, not a write target.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the natural fit for analysts who want T-SQL access to lakehouse data without learning Spark, as long as the workload never needs to write — which is exactly the boundary the warning node below exists to flag.

inputs: An ad hoc or BI-style read-only query against already-landed lakehouse Delta tables
processing: Connect a T-SQL client or Power BI DirectQuery to the SQL analytics endpoint
Query the same Delta tables the lakehouse's Spark session writes
outputs: Query results against current lakehouse table state, with no data movement or export
drill.example: A BI analyst runs an ad hoc T-SQL query against a gold-layer lakehouse table through the SQL analytics endpoint to validate a number before building a report, without touching Spark at all.
controls: No write attempts should ever be routed here — see the warning node
failureModes: Assuming the endpoint supports writes because it looks like a normal SQL database — see the dedicated warning node for this exact trap

nodes.label: Warehouse T-SQL
nodes.summary: Full governed T-SQL with multi-table ACID transactions — pick this when the workload writes and needs transactional semantics.
nodes.detail: Fabric Warehouse exposes a full T-SQL development surface including multi-table ACID transactions, stored procedures, and materialized views, over tables that are physically Delta and auto-published to OneLake. It is the right choice when a workload genuinely needs write access plus transactional guarantees that the read-only SQL analytics endpoint cannot provide.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the only one of the four engines offering full write-capable T-SQL with transactional semantics, so any workload with that specific requirement has effectively no substitute among the other three.

inputs: A write workload requiring multi-table transactional consistency, expressed as T-SQL
processing: Load and transform data with T-SQL CTAS, MERGE, and stored procedures inside a governed warehouse
Commit multi-table transactions as a single unit
outputs: A transactionally consistent warehouse whose tables are still open Delta files in OneLake
drill.example: A nightly load updates a fact table and three dimension tables inside one multi-table transaction, so a mid-load failure never leaves a partially-updated star schema visible to reports.
controls: Whether the workload actually uses the transaction boundary, or whether a simpler engine would suffice
failureModes: Choosing Warehouse for a purely read-only reporting workload that the SQL analytics endpoint could serve for free

nodes.label: KQL against Eventhouse
nodes.summary: High-volume time-series/telemetry querying — pick this when the data shape is streaming or log data, not relational.
nodes.detail: KQL (Kusto Query Language) queries an Eventhouse's KQL database, purpose-built for high-volume, time-series, log, and telemetry data with sub-second query latency, distinct in both language and data shape from the three T-SQL/Spark-SQL-family engines above.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is the branch that isn't really competing on skillset or write-capability — it's selected by data shape: relational/tabular data doesn't belong here, and time-series/telemetry data usually doesn't belong in the other three.

inputs: High-volume, time-series, log, or telemetry event data
processing: Query an Eventhouse KQL database using KQL rather than T-SQL or Spark SQL
outputs: Sub-second query results over recent and historical event data
drill.example: An operations team queries IoT sensor telemetry ingested through Eventstream into an Eventhouse, using KQL time-window aggregations that would be awkward to express as T-SQL joins.
controls: Whether the workload's data shape is genuinely time-series/event data versus relational, which is the real branch condition here
failureModes: Forcing relational reporting data into an Eventhouse just because KQL feels novel, when a lakehouse or warehouse fits the shape better

nodes.label: Trap: SQL analytics endpoint is read-only
nodes.summary: Attempting to write through the SQL analytics endpoint fails — it looks like a normal SQL surface but isn't.
nodes.detail: The SQL analytics endpoint exposes lakehouse Delta tables through T-SQL and looks, on the surface, like any writable SQL database. It is not: it is a read-only query surface. A workload that starts as read-only reporting and later grows a write requirement cannot simply add INSERT/UPDATE statements against the endpoint — it must move that write path to Spark SQL or Warehouse instead.
nodes.whyItMatters: This is an easy mistake specifically because the endpoint's T-SQL surface makes it feel writable; the failure is discovered only when a write statement is actually attempted, often well after the read-only design was assumed settled.

inputs: A workload originally designed as read-only against the SQL analytics endpoint that later needs to write
processing: Attempt an INSERT/UPDATE/MERGE against the endpoint (fails)
Recognize the endpoint is read-only by design
Reroute the write path to Spark SQL in a notebook or to Warehouse T-SQL
outputs: A corrected architecture with reads still against the endpoint (or the new write-capable engine) and writes routed to a write-capable surface
drill.example: A reporting workload built entirely against the SQL analytics endpoint later needs a scheduled correction job to patch bad rows; the fix has to be written as a Spark SQL notebook cell against the lakehouse, not as a T-SQL UPDATE against the endpoint.
controls: Confirm read/write requirements before committing an architecture to the SQL analytics endpoint alone
failureModes: Discovering the read-only limitation only when a write statement fails in production or during a late-stage requirement change
Working around it by writing directly to the underlying Delta files outside Fabric's managed paths, bypassing governance

edges.label: ad hoc T-SQL, read-only lakehouse data
if a write is later attempted

walkthrough.title: 1. Ask read/write, skillset, and data shape
walkthrough.explanation: The engine choice follows from whether the workload writes, what language the team knows, and whether the data is relational or time-series.

walkthrough.title: 2. Spark SQL for read/write transformation
walkthrough.explanation: Shares the notebook's Spark session with PySpark and Scala cells — the right fit whenever the workload does more than ad hoc querying.

walkthrough.title: 3. SQL analytics endpoint for read-only T-SQL
walkthrough.explanation: Auto-provisioned, zero-ETL T-SQL access to lakehouse Delta tables — but read-only, which the warning node explains.

walkthrough.title: 4. Warehouse for governed, transactional writes
walkthrough.explanation: The only branch offering full write-capable T-SQL with multi-table ACID transactions.

walkthrough.title: 5. KQL for time-series and telemetry data
walkthrough.explanation: Selected by data shape, not skillset — high-volume event data belongs in an Eventhouse, not a relational engine.

walkthrough.title: 6. Warning: the endpoint's T-SQL surface hides its read-only nature
walkthrough.explanation: A workload that grows a write requirement after being built against the SQL analytics endpoint has to move that write path elsewhere entirely.
